newsitem.title: BELGIUM: RENAULT FACES BOYCOTT OVER BELGIAN PLANT CLOSURE.
newsitem.headline: RENAULT FACES BOYCOTT OVER BELGIAN PLANT CLOSURE.

text.p: A decision by French carmaker Renault to close its Belgian assembly plant and move its activities to France and Spain is threatening to backfire with unions and politicians calling for a boycott of the make.
"This is my last Renault. What about you?," a placard by a Belgian Renault worker occupying the doomed plant said.
"They want to produce Renaults abroad? They should sell them abroad as well then," he said on Belgian television on Sunday.
Renault announced on Thursday that it would close the plant at Vilvoorde near Brussels in July as part of a strategy to cut overcapacity and restructure the group to improve profitability.

Karel Gacoms, a senior official with the BBTK metal workers union, said on television, "an important key (to resolving the issue) is now in the hands of consumers and French unions." He added consumers had already cancelled orders for Renault cars.
Gacoms said he would meet French union officials later on Sunday to discuss possible joint action.
French unions, fearing similar moves in France by a company more concerned with profits than jobs, are equally outraged by what they call a cynical Renault decision.
Belgian nationalist politicians were tough on Renault.

Bert Anciaux of the Volksunie party was quoted in the Belgian press as saying he would never again buy a Renault and urged all owners to tell Renault management. The Vlaams Blok party called for a boycott of all French products.
In Belgium Renault is a top three make, having sold just under 44,000 in 1996, coming after Volkswagen with about 78,500 units and Peugeot with some 57,000.
France is the country's third largest trading partner in the European Union with 1996 exports to Belgium worth an estimated 505 billion Belgian francs.

The closure, which will cost 3,100 workers and at least 1,000 at suppliers and subcontractors their jobs, has caused a storm of protests among Vilvoorde people and sparked angry words from Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, who lives in Vilvoorde.
Dehaene on Friday had denounced the decision as brutal, taken by "a head office...far away from the locality affected and independent of its social consequences."
But Renault has refused to go back on the move.

Its chief executive officer Louis Schweitzer said firmly after talks in Brussels on Saturday with government leaders of the Flanders region, where Vilvoorde is located, that Renault would not review the decision.

There now appears to be little the regional, and federal, government can do to stop Renault from closing the plant apart from bemoaning the harsh way in which the decision was announced and attacking Renault for procedural breaches.
Belgium is investigating whether to sue Renault for breaching rules on information and consultation of employees and which sanctions could be taken.
In the worst case Renault will face a heavy fine, but its decision to close Vilvoorde will remain intact.
On Monday workers meet for a general assembly at the occupied plant, where they are holding millions of francs worth of cars as bargaining chips, before a march on Brussels.

Dehaene said on Friday he would take up the matter with his French counterpart Alain Juppe again on Monday. On Thursday Juppe told him by telephone he would discuss the closure with the management of the partly state-owned carmaker.
France has a 46 percent stake in Renault, which expects to have suffered its first loss in 10 years in 1996 because of weak markets, high costs -- despite the launch of new models.
Renault said the Vilvoorde closure was part of a wider reorganisation and would save the company 825 million French francs ($144.5 million) a year, once completed.
